claim: Tupiocoris notatus is a 3-4 mm mirid bug (Miridae, Heteroptera) specialized to tobacco species and a few other solanaceous plants including Datura wrightii.
source: T. notatus is a free-living, 3–4 mm mirid bug (Miridae, Heteroptera) specialized to tobacco species and a few other solanaceous plants including Datura wrightii.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: Tupiocoris notatus is a piercing-sucking cell-content feeder that damages the surface of leaves without removing foliar material.
source: It is a piercing-sucking cell-content feeder that damages the surface of the leaves without removing foliar material.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section describing T. notatus feeding behavior.

claim: Infestation with T. notatus in nature does not decrease plant fitness despite resulting in damage to large portions of photosynthetically active leaf area.
source: In contrast, infestation with T. notatus in nature, surprisingly, does not decrease plant fitness (Kessler and Baldwin, 2004), despite resulting in damage to large portions of photosynthetically active leaf area.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kessler and Baldwin, 2004.

claim: Tissues around T. notatus feeding sites have increased rates of photosynthesis per chlorophyll content that may compensate for the damage caused by herbivore feeding.
source: Tissues around T. notatus feeding sites have increased rates of photosynthesis per chlorophyll content that may compensate for the damage caused by herbivore feeding, resulting from an active ingredient of the oral secretion of T. notatus which remains to be identified (Halitschke et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Halitschke et al., 2011.

claim: Three days of T. notatus feeding induced levels of the defense metabolites nicotine and caffeoylputrescine (CP), as well as trypsin proteinase inhibitor activity (TPI).
source: Three days of T. notatus feeding induced levels of the defense metabolites nicotine and caffeoylputrescine (CP), as well as trypsin proteinase inhibitor activity (TPI) (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-e.

claim: T. notatus feeding elevated the levels of jasmonic acid (JA), its precursor cis-(+)−12-oxophytodienoic acid (OPDA) and its bioactive isoleucine conjugate (JA-Ile).
source: T. notatus feeding also elevated the levels of jasmonic acid (JA), its precursor cis-(+)−12-oxophytodienoic acid (OPDA) and its bioactive isoleucine conjugate (JA-Ile) (Figure 1f–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f-h.

claim: T. notatus feeding caused a significant increase in salicylic acid (SA).
source: Interestingly, there was also a significant increase in salicylic acid (SA), but no influence on abscisic acid (ABA) (Figure 1i,j).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: T. notatus feeding had no influence on abscisic acid (ABA) levels.
source: Interestingly, there was also a significant increase in salicylic acid (SA), but no influence on abscisic acid (ABA) (Figure 1i,j).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: JA and JA-Ile levels triggered by T. notatus feeding remained elevated for up to six days when mirids were confined to feed on a single leaf.
source: JA and JA-Ile levels triggered by T. notatus feeding remained elevated for up to six days when mirids were confined to feed on a single leaf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: N. attenuata's response to T. notatus involves activation of JA signaling and downstream defense responses.
source: These results demonstrate that N. attenuata's response to T. notatus involves activation of JA signaling and downstream defense responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing increased JA, JA-Ile, OPDA, and defense metabolites.

claim: Total soluble protein (TSP) levels decreased with time in a clipcage but mirid feeding did not have a significant influence.
source: TSP levels decreased with time in a clipcage but mirid feeding did not have a significant influence (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T. notatus feeding did not cause significant changes in starch, sucrose, glucose or fructose levels when mirids were confined to a single leaf.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any significant changes in starch, sucrose, glucose or fructose (Figure 2c–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c-f.

claim: Photosynthesis was significantly reduced in T. notatus attacked leaves.
source: Although we did not observe changes in carbohydrate levels, photosynthesis was significantly reduced in attacked leaves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mirid feeding had no effect on chlorophyll contents when confined to a single leaf.
source: In contrast, mirid feeding had no effect on chlorophyll contents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: When entire plants were heavily infested, TSP levels decreased after mirid feeding.
source: When entire plants were heavily infested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), changes in nutrient levels in the plant became apparent only for TSP levels, which decreased after mirid feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Levels of starch, sucrose, glucose and fructose were not affected by mirid feeding during whole-plant attack.
source: Conversely, levels of starch, sucrose, glucose and fructose were not affected by mirid feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c-f.

claim: Both chlorophyll contents and photosynthetic rates significantly decreased after T. notatus whole-plant attack.
source: Both chlorophyll contents and photosynthetic rates significantly decreased after T. notatus whole-plant attack (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a-c.

claim: When entire plants were severely attacked, TSP levels of attacked leaves decreased, but sugar and starch contents remained unchanged.
source: In contrast, during a more extreme mirid infestation in which entire plants were severely attacked, TSP levels of attacked leaves decreased, but sugar and starch contents remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results from whole-plant infestation experiments.

claim: An allocation of nutrients from unattacked to attacked tissue may explain the observation that even heavy T. notatus feeding only marginally influenced nutrient levels in attacked leaves.
source: An allocation of nutrients from unattacked to attacked tissue may explain the observation that even heavy T. notatus feeding only marginally influenced nutrient levels in attacked leaves.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Mirid feeding likely influences the source/sink relationships of the host plant.
source: If this inference is correct, then mirid feeding likely influences the source/sink relationships of the host plant.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the nutrient allocation hypothesis.

claim: Mirid feeding significantly increased the accumulation of NaCKX5 transcripts, which code for a CK oxidase/dehydrogenase responsible for CK degradation.
source: When entire plants were attacked, mirid feeding significantly increased the accumulation of NaCKX5 transcripts, which code for a CK oxidase/dehydrogenase responsible for CK degradation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Transcript levels of NaZOG2, which codes for a CK glucosyltransferase responsible for CK inactivation, increased after mirid feeding.
source: Transcript levels of NaZOG2, which codes for a CK glucosyltransferase responsible for CK inactivation, as well as transcripts of NaLOG4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), which is involved in CK biosynthesis, also increased after mirid feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Transcripts of NaLOG4, which is involved in CK biosynthesis, increased after mirid feeding.
source: Transcript levels of NaZOG2, which codes for a CK glucosyltransferase responsible for CK inactivation, as well as transcripts of NaLOG4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), which is involved in CK biosynthesis, also increased after mirid feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Transcript levels of the isopentenyltransferase NaIPT5, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of CK biosynthesis, were reduced after mirid feeding.
source: In contrast, transcript levels of the isopentenyltransferase NaIPT5, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of CK biosynthesis, were reduced after mirid feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: T. notatus feeding did not change levels of the CK response regulator NaRRA5.
source: T. notatus feeding did not change levels of the CK response regulator NaRRA5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Overall leaf CK contents gradually increased over time when entire plants were infested with T. notatus.
source: When entire plants were infested with T. notatus, overall leaf CK contents gradually increased over time (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Levels of cis-zeatin (cZ) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack during whole-plant infestation.
source: Levels of cis-zeatin (cZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), cis-zeatin riboside (cZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), trans-zeatin (tZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Levels of cis-zeatin riboside (cZR) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack during whole-plant infestation.
source: Levels of cis-zeatin (cZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), cis-zeatin riboside (cZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), trans-zeatin (tZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d.

claim: Levels of trans-zeatin (tZ) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack during whole-plant infestation.
source: Levels of cis-zeatin (cZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), cis-zeatin riboside (cZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), trans-zeatin (tZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Levels of trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack during whole-plant infestation.
source: Levels of cis-zeatin (cZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), cis-zeatin riboside (cZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), trans-zeatin (tZ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and trans-zeatin riboside (tZR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e) were significantly higher after T. notatus attack.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2e.

claim: Levels of N6-isopentenyladenine (IP) remained unaffected by mirid feeding during whole-plant infestation.
source: In contrast, levels of N6-isopentenyladenine (IP) remained unaffected by mirid feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c) and levels of N6-isopentenyladenosine (IPR) decreased in attacked leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Levels of N6-isopentenyladenosine (IPR) decreased in attacked leaves during whole-plant infestation.
source: In contrast, levels of N6-isopentenyladenine (IP) remained unaffected by mirid feeding (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c) and levels of N6-isopentenyladenosine (IPR) decreased in attacked leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2f.

claim: The decrease in IPR levels was significant in the first 24 hr after the initiation of mirid attack and disappeared at later harvest times.
source: This decrease was significant in the first 24 hr after the initiation of mirid attack and disappeared at later harvest times (p<0.05 in TukeyHSD post hoc test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When mirids were only allowed to feed on a single leaf, there was no change in levels of summed CKs over the whole time series.
source: When mirids were only allowed to feed on a single leaf, we did not observe changes in levels of summed CKs over the whole time series (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Bonferroni-corrected t-tests of single time point revealed increased CK levels at the last time point harvested, after 144 hr of feeding.
source: However, Bonferroni-corrected t-tests of single time point revealed increased levels at the last time point harvested, after 144 hr of feeding (tt: p=0.026).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant increase in cZ during single-leaf feeding.
source: There was a significant increase in cZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c), but levels of cZR decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Levels of cZR decreased during single-leaf feeding.
source: There was a significant increase in cZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c), but levels of cZR decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3f.

claim: IP levels were significantly higher overall after single-leaf feeding, although pairwise comparisons for each time point did not reveal significant changes at any given time point.
source: IP levels, which did not change during whole-plant feeding, were significantly higher overall after single-leaf feeding, although pairwise comparisons for each time point did not reveal significant changes at any given time point.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: tZ, tZR and IPR remained unaffected by mirid feeding when only single leaves were attacked.
source: tZ, tZR and IPR remained unaffected by mirid feeding when only single leaves were attacked (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d,g,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d,g,h.

claim: In both experiments overall CK levels remained unchanged or were increased, despite the concomitant increases in transcripts of genes related to CK degradation.
source: Interestingly, in both experiments overall CK levels remained unchanged or were increased, despite the concomitant increases in transcripts of genes related to CK degradation.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the experimental results.

claim: CKs are involved in the observed nutritional stability during mirid feeding.
source: From these results, we infer that CKs are involved in the observed nutritional stability during mirid feeding; this hypothesis prompted a more detailed analysis of the origin of these CKs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: T. notatus contains very high levels of IP and IPR in extracts from the insect bodies.
source: We found very high levels of IP and IPR in extracts from the insect bodies (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Concentrations of IPR in T. notatus were comparable to those in leaves (around 1 pmol per g fresh mass (FM)).
source: While concentrations of IPR were comparable to those in leaves (around 1 pmol per g fresh mass (FM)), concentrations of IP exceeded those of leaves by up to three orders of magnitude: while levels in leaves ranged from 0.01 to 0.1 pmol g FM−1, levels in insects were usually between 1 and 5 pmol g FM−1 and attained values as high as 16 pmol g FM−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CK levels in insects and leaves.

claim: Concentrations of IP in T. notatus exceeded those of leaves by up to three orders of magnitude.
source: While concentrations of IPR were comparable to those in leaves (around 1 pmol per g fresh mass (FM)), concentrations of IP exceeded those of leaves by up to three orders of magnitude: while levels in leaves ranged from 0.01 to 0.1 pmol g FM−1, levels in insects were usually between 1 and 5 pmol g FM−1 and attained values as high as 16 pmol g FM−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CK levels in insects and leaves.

claim: Insects collected from N. attenuata plants in their natural habitat at a field site in Utah, USA, contained high amounts of IP: in a pooled sample of ten insects, 18.26 pmol IP per g FM-1 was measured.
source: Insects collected from N. attenuata plants in their natural habitat at a field site in Utah, USA, also contained high amounts of IP: in a pooled sample of ten insects, we measured 18.26 pmol IP per g FM-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from field-collected insects.

claim: Mirids contained high IP and IPR levels in their bodies independently of their sex, developmental stage, or food source.
source: Mirids contained high IP and IPR levels in their bodies independently of their sex, developmental stage, or food source (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: IP concentration in nymphs was about half as high as in adult males and females, but nymphs still had concentration several times those found in leaves.
source: The sole significant difference was that IP concentration in nymphs was about half as high as in adult males and females, but nymphs still had concentration several times those found in leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Insects raised on artificial diet had IP levels in their body that were not different from levels in insects raised on plants.
source: Insects raised on artificial diet had IP levels in their body that were not different from levels in insects raised on plants; IPR levels were also unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4b.

claim: IP and IPR found in T. notatus body could be used by the mirid to counter the decrease in IP levels in attacked leaves that is commonly observed in response to long-term JA elicitation or M. sexta feeding.
source: Although the source of CKs in T. notatus remains unknown, we hypothesize that IP and IPR found in T. notatus body could be used by the mirid to counter the decrease in IP levels in attacked leaves that is commonly observed in response to long-term JA elicitation or M. sexta feeding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: After four days of continuous feeding by 15N-labeled T. notatus on 14N-grown plants, detectable amounts of 15N-labeled IP (and IPR) were found in the leaves.
source: After four days of continuous feeding, we found detectable amounts of 15N-labeled IP (and IPR) in the leaves (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3): around 2.35 fmol [15N5]-IP per g FM, which represent the 3.3% of the [15N5]/[14N5]-IP ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 15N-labeling experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: 15N-labelled IP and IPR found in leaves could only have originated from the insects, as the natural abundance of 15N is below 0.4%, and IP (or IPR) with five 15N would occur about once in a trillion molecules.
source: [15N5]-labelled IP and IPR could only have originated from the insects, as the natural abundance of 15N is below 0.4%, and IP (or IPR) with five 15N would occur about once in a trillion molecules.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of natural isotope abundance and statistical probability.

claim: One mirid feeding on a leaf for five days could account for a transfer of at least 0.12 fmol IP per g FM−1.
source: From these values, one mirid feeding on a leaf for five days could account for a transfer of at least 0.12 fmol IP per g FM−1 (Supplementary file 1), assuming that CK transport, degradation or conversion to other CK forms can be excluded.
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental data.

claim: In the reverse experiment using 15N-grown plants and 14N-labeled insects, after 5 days, an average of 48% of the [15N5]/[14N5]-IP ratio was 14N labeled and therefore originating from the insects.
source: After 5 days, an average of 48% of the [15N5]/[14N5]-IP ratio was 14N labeled and therefore originating from the insects (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: IPR transfer from the insect to the plant was detected after 24 hr and accounted to 19% of the [15N5]/[14N5]-IP ratio after 5 d in the stronger induction setup.
source: In this stronger induction setup, IPR transfer from the insect to the plant was also already detected after 24 hr and accounted to 19% of the [15N5]/[14N5]-IP ratio after 5 d (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large amounts (high signal intensity) of IP were found mainly from the oral secretions (from the sugar solution that mirids had fed on) and much lower amounts in the frass of the mirids (from the surface wash).
source: We found large amounts (high signal intensity) of IP mainly from the oral secretions (from the sugar solution that mirids had fed on) and much lower amounts in the frass of the mirids (from the surface wash) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IPR was found in oral secretions and in frass in similar amounts.
source: IPR was found in oral secretions and in frass in similar amounts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: T. notatus is able to transfer CKs (mainly IP) to its host plant.
source: These results clearly demonstrate that T. notatus is able to transfer CKs (mainly IP) to its host plant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 15N-labeling experiments and oral secretion analysis.

claim: The most likely means of CK transfer would be via the salivary secretion produced during feeding.
source: The most likely means of transfer would be via the salivary secretion produced during feeding, although we cannot rule out a smaller contribution of feces, which are sticky and tend to cover infested leaves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing high IP in oral secretions.

claim: In nature, T. notatus feeds on young N. attenuata tissues, such as younger stem leaves and young growing leaves.
source: In nature, T. notatus feeds on young N. attenuata tissues, such as younger stem leaves and young growing leaves.
evidence: This is based on observations of damage distributions in nature and glasshouse.

claim: The feeding pattern of T. notatus on young leaves was inferred from the damage distributions observed on plants in both nature and the glasshouse, as well as in two-choice assays.
source: This feeding pattern was inferred from the damage distributions observed on plants in both nature and the glasshouse (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), as well as in two-choice assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The young leaves preferred by T. notatus are typically rich in CKs.
source: The young leaves preferred by T. notatus are typically rich in CKs (Brütting et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brütting et al., 2017.

claim: T. notatus prefers leaves of i-ovipt plants which have been treated with DEX and therefore have higher levels of CKs.
source: T. notatus prefers leaves of i-ovipt plants which have been treated with DEX and therefore have higher levels of CKs (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: If T. notatus is given the choice between empty vector (EV) and irchk2/3 plants, mirids show a strong preference for EV plants, as shown in the lower damage levels on irchk2/3 plants.
source: If T. notatus is given the choice between empty vector (EV) and irchk2/3 plants, mirids show a strong preference for EV plants, as shown in the lower damage levels on irchk2/3 plants (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Mirid attack caused necrotic lesions in irchk2/3 plants, comparable to a pathogen-induced hypersensitive response, whereas this did not occur in WT, EV or i-ovipt plants.
source: Furthermore, we found pronounced differences in the reaction of the plants to the damage caused by T. notatus feeding. Mirid attack caused necrotic lesions in irchk2/3 plants, comparable to a pathogen-induced hypersensitive response, whereas this did not occur in WT, EV or i-ovipt plants (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: i-ovipt plants had higher concentrations of protein, free amino acids, glucose and fructose than did irchk2/3 plants.
source: However, i-ovipt plants had higher concentrations of protein, free amino acids, glucose and fructose than did irchk2/3 plants (Figure 7a,b,d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a,b,d,e.

claim: Starch and sucrose did not differ among the transgenic lines.
source: Starch and sucrose did not differ among the lines (Figure 7c,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c,f.

claim: The i-ovipt plants tended to have higher nutrient levels than did EV plants but the results were only statistically significant for glucose concentrations.
source: The i-ovipt plants tended to have higher nutrient levels than did EV plants but the results were only statistically significant for glucose concentrations (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: irchk2/3 plants tended to have lower nutrient levels compared to EV, but these were only significantly lower for fructose concentrations.
source: In contrast, irchk2/3 plants tended to have lower nutrient levels compared to EV, but these were only significantly lower for fructose concentrations (Figure 7e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: CKs play a dual role in the T. notatus-N. attenuata interaction: as important determinants of tissue palatability for T. notatus by enhancing nutrient contents, but also as important tolerance factors that allow plants to suffer negligible or lower fitness consequences of mirid attack than they would otherwise.
source: From these results, we conclude that CKs play a dual role in the T. notatus-N. attenuata interaction: as important determinants of tissue palatability for T. notatus by enhancing nutrient contents, but also as important tolerance factors that allow plants to suffer negligible or lower fitness consequences of mirid attack than they would otherwise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with transgenic plants.

claim: This work provides evidence that a free-living insect uses CKs to manipulate source/sink relationships to increase food quality and minimize the fitness consequences of its feeding.
source: We infer that this free-living insect uses CKs to manipulate source/sink relationships to increase food quality and minimize the fitness consequences of its feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: This work provides the first clear demonstration of CK transfer from an insect to a plant.
source: We unambiguously demonstrated that T. notatus transfers two types of CKs, IP and its riboside IPR, to N. attenuata providing the first clear demonstration of CK transfer from an insect to a plant.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: IP has been generally considered one of the most active natural CKs based on classical activity assays.
source: IP has been generally considered one of the most active natural CKs based on classical activity assays (Gyulai and Heszky, 1994; Sakakibara, 2006) and high concentrations of IP have been previously reported in plant-manipulating endophytic insects, like leaf miners and gall-formers (Engelbrecht, 1968; Engelbrecht et al., 1969; Mapes and Davies, 2001; Straka et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2012; Body et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gyulai and Heszky, 1994; Sakakibara, 2006.

claim: High concentrations of IP have been previously reported in plant-manipulating endophytic insects, like leaf miners and gall-formers.
source: IP has been generally considered one of the most active natural CKs based on classical activity assays (Gyulai and Heszky, 1994; Sakakibara, 2006) and high concentrations of IP have been previously reported in plant-manipulating endophytic insects, like leaf miners and gall-formers (Engelbrecht, 1968; Engelbrecht et al., 1969; Mapes and Davies, 2001; Straka et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2012; Body et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Engelbrecht, 1968; Engelbrecht et al., 1969; Mapes and Davies, 2001; Straka et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2012; Body et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2013.

claim: Oral secretions, and in much lower amounts, frass of T. notatus, contained IP and IPR, thus providing a possible means of transfer.
source: We also showed that oral secretions, and in much lower amounts, frass of T. notatus, contained IP and IPR, thus providing a possible means of transfer.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results from the oral secretion and frass analysis.

claim: Concentrations of total CK content of N. attenuata leaves steadily increased during long-term T. notatus feeding, consistent with the observation that mirids transferred CKs to plants.
source: Concentrations of total CK content of N. attenuata leaves steadily increased during long-term T. notatus feeding, consistent with the observation that mirids transferred CKs to plants.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results linking CK transfer to increased CK levels.

claim: The overall reconfiguration of the transcriptional activity of genes involved in CK degradation, inactivation, and biosynthesis upon T. notatus feeding did not correlate with the apparent changes in CK concentrations.
source: The overall reconfiguration of the transcriptional activity of genes involved in CK degradation, inactivation, and biosynthesis upon T. notatus feeding did not correlate with the apparent changes in CK concentrations.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing transcript and metabolite data.

claim: N. attenuata might activate a type of CK detoxification in response to mirid feeding and CK introduction.
source: This suggests that N. attenuata might activate a type of CK detoxification in response to mirid feeding and CK introduction.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the mismatch between transcript and metabolite changes.

claim: After five days of whole-plant infestation, roughly half of the total IP in attacked leaves originated from mirids.
source: This was surprising, considering that we estimated that after five days of whole-plant infestation, roughly half of the total IP in attacked leaves originated from mirids.
evidence: This is based on the 15N-labeling experiment results.

claim: Understanding to what extent the observed changes in cytokinin signaling result from mirid-mediated CK transfer is complicated by the fact that CK levels respond as part of the herbivory-inducible defense signaling.
source: Understanding to what extent the observed changes in cytokinin signaling result from mirid-mediated CK transfer is further complicated by the fact that CK levels respond as part of the herbivory-inducible defense signaling (Schäfer et al., 2015a; Schäfer et al., 2015c; Brütting et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schäfer et al., 2015a; Schäfer et al., 2015c; Brütting et al., 2017.

claim: The dual role of CKs in plant growth and defense highlights the complexity of the fine regulation of CKs needed to regulate plant physiological responses.
source: The dual role of CKs in plant growth and defense highlights the complexity of the fine regulation of CKs needed to regulate plant physiological responses.
evidence: This is a general statement based on the experimental observations.

claim: Not only CK quantities, but also CK structures, and the hormonal balance with other phytohormones may influence changes in metabolism upon insect feeding.
source: Not only CK quantities, but also CK structures, and the hormonal balance with other phytohormones may influence changes in metabolism upon insect feeding (Giron et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giron et al., 2013.

claim: Demonstrable effects on host plants induced by endophytic insects include alterations of plant morphology, changes in the nutritional quality of the affected tissues and the inactivation of plant defenses surrounding the attack sites.
source: Demonstrable effects on host plants induced by endophytic insects include alterations of plant morphology, changes in the nutritional quality of the affected tissues and the inactivation of plant defenses surrounding the attack sites (Giron et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giron et al., 2016.

claim: Control of the nutritional quality of the infested tissues seems to be a common feature of all endophytic insect-plant interactions.
source: Whereas alterations of plant morphology are associated with only some endophytic insects, for example gall-formers, control of the nutritional quality of the infested tissues seems to be a common feature of all endophytic insect-plant interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of endophytic insect-plant interactions.

claim: Wounding and application of oral secretions (OS) of M. sexta as well as M. sexta feeding reduced glucose and fructose concentrations by inhibiting soluble invertases.
source: Previous studies in N. attenuata showed that wounding and application of oral secretions (OS) of M. sexta as well as M. sexta feeding reduced glucose and fructose concentrations by inhibiting soluble invertases.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: Such reductions in glucose and fructose are JA-dependent, and abrogated in transgenic lines impaired in JA production.
source: Such reductions are JA-dependent, and abrogated in transgenic lines impaired in JA production (Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Machado et al., 2015.

claim: A negative influence of jasmonates on plant primary metabolism has been suggested by studies in a number of other plants.
source: A negative influence of jasmonates on plant primary metabolism has also been suggested by studies in a number of other plants (Babst et al., 2005; Skrzypek et al., 2005; van Dam and Oomen, 2008; Hanik et al., 2010; Tytgat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Babst et al., 2005; Skrzypek et al., 2005; van Dam and Oomen, 2008; Hanik et al., 2010; Tytgat et al., 2013.

claim: The fact that T. notatus feeding activated JA-signaling, but did not negatively influence soluble monosaccharide concentrations, suggested that an additional counterbalancing alteration in the primary metabolism of N. attenuata occurs during T. notatus feeding.
source: Hence, the fact that T. notatus feeding activated JA-signaling, but did not negatively influence soluble monosaccharide concentrations, suggested that an additional counterbalancing alteration in the primary metabolism of N. attenuata occurs during T. notatus feeding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing T. notatus effects with known JA effects.

claim: Wounding and M. sexta OS application results in a 91% reduction of total soluble proteins (TSPs) in young rosette leaves.
source: Similar to what has been observed for carbohydrates, wounding and M. sexta OS application results in a 91% reduction of total soluble proteins (TSPs) in young rosette leaves (Ullmann-Zeunert et al., 2013), the same leaf stage used in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ullmann-Zeunert et al., 2013.

claim: After 144 hr of continuous T. notatus infestation, TSP reductions were only ca. 75%.
source: After 144 hr of continuous T. notatus infestation, during which proteins should be heavily depleted by mechanical cell-content damage – in contrast to the minor damage associated with OS elicitation (Halitschke et al., 2001) – TSP reductions were only ca. 75%.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the whole-plant infestation experiments.

claim: A smaller T. notatus infestation (twenty mirids confined on a single leaf) did not change TSP contents at all during 144 hr of continuous feeding.
source: More surprisingly, a smaller T. notatus infestation (twenty mirids confined on a single leaf) did not change TSP contents at all during 144 hr of continuous feeding.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the single-leaf infestation experiments.

claim: Microarray analysis that compared expression patterns induced by T. notatus and M. sexta revealed that mirid-specific transcriptional responses occurred largely in primary metabolism.
source: These results are consistent with microarray analysis that compared expression patterns induced by T. notatus and M. sexta, which revealed that mirid-specific transcriptional responses occurred largely in primary metabolism (Voelckel and Baldwin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voelckel and Baldwin, 2004.

claim: During T. notatus feeding, plant's primary metabolism seems to be influenced by mechanisms different from the classical JA-mediated herbivory and wound responses.
source: Thus, during T. notatus feeding, plant's primary metabolism seems to be influenced by mechanisms different from the classical JA-mediated herbivory and wound responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Reduced photosynthetic rate is a general response observed in a number of plant-insect interactions as well as in N. attenuata.
source: Reduced photosynthetic rate is a general response observed in a number of plant-insect interactions (Zhou et al., 2015) as well as in N. attenuata.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: Wounding and elicitation with M. sexta OS rapidly decrease photosynthetic CO2 assimilation and this reduction is mediated by the JA-precursor OPDA.
source: Wounding and elicitation with M. sexta OS rapidly decrease photosynthetic CO2 assimilation and this reduction is mediated by the JA-precursor OPDA (Meza-Canales et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meza-Canales et al., 2017.

claim: The discrepancy between this work and results from Halitschke et al. (2011) likely results from differences in the experimental protocols used.
source: We think that the discrepancy between our work and results from Halitschke et al. (2011) likely results from differences in the experimental protocols used: (1) we used a very heavy infestation, (2) the leaf area used to measure the photosynthetic rates of mirid-attacked leaves included both damaged and undamaged areas, (3) we did not normalize photosynthetic rates to intact undamaged leaf tissue.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: The reduction in the overall photosynthetic rates observed during T. notatus feeding was not consistent with unchanged starch and sugar levels and suggests the inhibition of senescence and/or transport of nutrients to the attacked leaves.
source: In any case, the reduction in the overall photosynthetic rates observed during T. notatus feeding was not consistent with unchanged starch and sugar levels and, together with the observation that T. notatus transfers CK during feeding, suggests the inhibition of senescence and/or transport of nutrients to the attacked leaves.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: T. notatus feeding activated N. attenuata JA-dependent defense pathways in a way consistent with previous studies.
source: We showed that T. notatus feeding activated N. attenuata JA-dependent defense pathways in a way consistent with previous studies; the increases in defense metabolites induced by T. notatus feeding were comparable to those elicited by M. sexta attack (Kessler and Baldwin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kessler and Baldwin, 2004.

claim: T. notatus is well-adapted to the specialized metabolism of N. attenuata; it prefers wild-type plants which are less susceptible to invasion by other herbivores, rather than those impaired in JA biosynthesis with reduced defense metabolites.
source: T. notatus is well-adapted to the specialized metabolism of N. attenuata; it prefers wild-type plants which are less susceptible to invasion by other herbivores, rather than those impaired in JA biosynthesis with reduced defense metabolites (Fragoso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fragoso et al., 2014.

claim: The detoxification ability of T. notatus is suggested by the observation that it accumulates transcripts encoding detoxification enzymes in response to JA-dependent defenses.
source: Insects counter the presence of toxic metabolites in their host plants by detoxification or sequestration of toxic substances (Heckel, 2014), and the detoxification ability of T. notatus is suggested by the observation that it accumulates transcripts encoding detoxification enzymes in response to JA-dependent defenses (Crava et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heckel, 2014 and Crava et al., 2016.

claim: Down-regulation of plant defense may not benefit T. notatus as much as its manipulation of its host's nutritional status.
source: This fact, togheter with the finding that defense pathways were not down-regulated during the T. notatus feeding, point out that down-regulation of plant defense may not benefit T. notatus as much as its manipulation of its host's nutritional status.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: T. notatus is attracted to quercetin.
source: For example, T. notatus is attracted to quercetin (Roda et al., 2003), and some related phenolic compounds are influenced by CK levels (Schäfer et al., 2015b; Brütting et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roda et al., 2003.

claim: Some phenolic compounds related to quercetin are influenced by CK levels.
source: For example, T. notatus is attracted to quercetin (Roda et al., 2003), and some related phenolic compounds are influenced by CK levels (Schäfer et al., 2015b; Brütting et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schäfer et al., 2015b; Brütting et al., 2017.

claim: Nutrient levels of transgenic lines correlated with T. notatus preference.
source: Consistent with the primary metabolism hypothesis, we showed that nutrient levels of transgenic lines correlated with T. notatus preference.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing nutrient levels and feeding preferences.

claim: T. notatus damage distribution on whole plants is concentrated on young, CK-rich and nutrient-rich tissues.
source: This inferred preference for nutrients is also consistent with T. notatus damage distribution on whole plants, which is concentrated on young, CK-rich and nutrient-rich tissues.
evidence: This is based on experimental data on damage distribution.

claim: Young, CK-rich and nutrient-rich tissues are also better defended.
source: These tissues are also better defended (Brütting et al., 2017) suggesting a possible trade-off between palatability and anti-digestive effects of the diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brütting et al., 2017.

claim: Specialized detoxification mechanisms likely allow T. notatus to feed with impunity on otherwise well-defended tissues.
source: However, specialized detoxification mechanisms likely allow T. notatus to feed with impunity on otherwise well-defended tissues (Crava et al., 2016), thus allowing T. notatus's feeding choice to reflect the nutritional quality, rather than the defensive status, of its host.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crava et al., 2016.

claim: This work provides evidence that a free-living insect transfers CKs which manipulates its host plant's metabolism, likely for its own benefit.
source: Our results provide evidence that a free-living insect transfers CKs which manipulates its host plant's metabolism, likely for its own benefit.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: CK-mediated plant manipulation strategies have only been known so far from endophytic insects.
source: CK-mediated plant manipulation strategies have only been known so far from endophytic insects (Giron et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Giron et al., 2016.

claim: The low mobility and intimate associations of endophytic insects with their host plants provides the selective environment for the evolution of mechanisms that allow them to manipulate host plant physiology and/or morphology.
source: The low mobility and intimate associations of endophytic insects with their host plants provides the selective environment for the evolution of mechanisms that allow them to manipulate host plant physiology and/or morphology.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of endophytic insect ecology.

claim: Species known for CK-dependent manipulation of host plants are not closely related to each other, and span several orders: Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, Hemiptera and Diptera.
source: Species known for CK-dependent manipulation of host plants are not closely related to each other, and span several orders: Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, Hemiptera and Diptera.
evidence: This is a summary of knowledge about CK-manipulating insects.

claim: The fact that species from different orders have developed similar mechanism of plant manipulation suggests either an ancient evolutionary origin or a convergent evolutionary trait.
source: The fact that species from different orders have developed similar mechanism of plant manipulation suggests either an ancient evolutionary origin or a convergent evolutionary trait.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on phylogenetic considerations.

claim: CK-dependent manipulation is more widespread than previously thought, and is also shared with free-living insects like T. notatus.
source: We propose that such CK-dependent manipulation is more widespread than previously thought, and is also shared with free-living insects like T. notatus.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: CKs transferred by T. notatus could originate from its host plant and be sequestered by the insect but also they could be synthesized by the insect itself or its associate endosymbionts.
source: CKs transferred by T. notatus could originate from its host plant and be sequestered by the insect but also they could be synthesized by the insect itself or its associate endosymbionts.
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of possible CK origins.

claim: CKs are also produced by organisms other than plants, like fungi, bacteria and nematodes.
source: In fact, CKs are also produced by organisms other than plants, like fungi (Chanclud et al., 2016), bacteria (Costacurta and Vanderleyden, 1995) and nematodes (Siddique et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chanclud et al., 2016; Costacurta and Vanderleyden, 1995; Siddique et al., 2015.

claim: IP and IPR can be derived from tRNA, and this suggests that the substrate for CK biosynthesis is shared by all organisms.
source: It is thought that IP and IPR can be derived from tRNA, and this suggests that the substrate for CK biosynthesis is shared by all organisms (Persson et al., 1994), virtually enabling insects to produce CKs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 1994.

claim: The most recent studies on CK-mediated manipulation of plant physiology by insects suggested a role of endosymbiotic bacteria in CK production.
source: The most recent studies on CK-mediated manipulation of plant physiology by insects suggested a role of endosymbiotic bacteria in CK production (Kaiser et al., 2010; Giron et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaiser et al., 2010; Giron et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: Antibiotic feeding experiments have revealed that endosymbionts like Wolbachia are the most likely producers of CKs in the leaf-miner P. blancardella.
source: Antibiotic feeding experiments have revealed that endosymbionts like Wolbachia are the most likely producers of CKs in the leaf-miner P. blancardella (Kaiser et al., 2010; Body et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaiser et al., 2010; Body et al., 2013.

claim: Wolbachia is unlikely responsible for CK production in T. notatus, as Wolbachia was not detected in mirids from the same glasshouse colony used in the experiments, and was identified only very rarely from insects collected from the field.
source: Yet, this bacterium is unlikely responsible for CK production in T. notatus, as Wolbachia was not be detected in mirids from the same glasshouse colony used in our experiments, and was identified only very rarely from insects collected from the field (Adam et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adam et al., 2017.

claim: Free-living phytophagous insects are thought not to manipulate their host plant's physiology to enhance the nutritional quality of their diet, as they are free to move to the best feeding locations on a plant.
source: Free-living phytophagous insects are thought not to manipulate their host plant's physiology to enhance the nutritional quality of their diet, as they are free to move to the best feeding locations on a plant.
evidence: This is a statement of conventional thinking in the field.

claim: This work provides evidence of the ability of a free-living insect to introduce CKs into their host during feeding to maintain a better nutritional environment.
source: This work provides evidence of the ability of a free-living insect to introduce CKs into their host during feeding to maintain a better nutritional environment.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: This mechanism may be commonly found in other free-living species and it combines the benefits of the two different lifestyles: the ability to move, hide and choose the best feeding locations, and to manipulate the host plant via CK-transfer.
source: We suggest that this mechanism may be commonly found in other free-living species and that it combines the benefits of the two different lifestyles: the ability to move, hide and choose the best feeding locations, and to manipulate the host plant via CK-transfer.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Clarifying the details of the origins of the T. notatus-transferred CKs and studying their role in nature will provide new insights into the complex interactions that occur during plant-herbivore interactions.
source: Clarifying the details of the origins of the T. notatus-transferred CKs and studying their role in nature will provide new insights into the complex interactions that occur during plant-herbivore interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Using 15N-isotope labeling, the CK N6-isopentenyladenine (IP) is transferred from insects to plants via their oral secretions.
source: Using 15N-isotope labeling, we demonstrate that the CK N6-isopentenyladenine (IP) is transferred from insects to plants via their oral secretions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: In the field, T. notatus preferentially attacks leaves with transgenically increased CK levels.
source: In the field, T. notatus preferentially attacks leaves with transgenically increased CK levels; plants with abrogated CK-perception are less tolerant of T. notatus feeding damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Plants with abrogated CK-perception are less tolerant of T. notatus feeding damage.
source: In the field, T. notatus preferentially attacks leaves with transgenically increased CK levels; plants with abrogated CK-perception are less tolerant of T. notatus feeding damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Feeding by the free-living herbivore Tupiocoris notatus on Nicotiana attenuata is characterized by stable nutrient levels, increased CK levels and alterations in CK-related transcript levels in attacked leaves, in striking similarity to endophytic insects.
source: Here we show that feeding by the free-living herbivore Tupiocoris notatus on Nicotiana attenuata is characterized by stable nutrient levels, increased CK levels and alterations in CK-related transcript levels in attacked leaves, in striking similarity to endophytic insects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.
